https://www.politico.eu/article/von-der-.text: STRASBOURG — Ursula von der Leyen has declared herself an AI “optimist.” Yet in the face of rising warnings of the technology’s threats to humanity, the European Commission president on Wednesday sounded far more like a realist — and one with limited room for maneuver . Von der Leyen didn’t shy away from the topic in her State of the European Union address, calling AI one of the “two tipping points of our time” and acknowledging the dangers it poses. "The warnings about the future of AI should make us more serious about safety," said key European Parliament AI lawmaker Axel Voss after the speech, touting von der Leyen's focus on "Europe's human-centered approach to AI." Advertisement Advertisement Still, the Commission president's most concrete response to recent calls by top Silicon Valley bosses to pause AI development was a cordial invitation to join her in a “discussion” on the matter. And while citing the EU’s standing AI rules as a possible building block for global regulations, von der Leyen didn’t use her much-anticipated speech to call on fellow world leaders — particularly U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping — to come together to act. Her diffidence risks turning Europe into a bystander amid a global scramble over calls to regulate frontier AI, which the U.S. leader has dismissed as a “hoax” — just ahead of a high-level summit between Trump and Xi that will likely explore how to set global standards on AI safety. Von der Leyen identified “the right diagnosis” in her speech, said Max Reddel, CEO of the Arq Foundation, a Brussels-based think tank focused on AI. But, he added, “the question is whether we can move at the speed and decisiveness she calls for.” In her speech, von der Leyen had to cater to two demands: that Europe stay competitive in the global AI race while also meeting the moment on global AI safety — a frenzy sparked by a warning from a former Anthropic engineer that AI could lead to the end of the human race. Von der Leyen said she was an “optimist” that AI could benefit humanity, but noted that “risks have sharply come into focus.” Advertisement Advertisement Europe also finds itself in a bind in addressing AI safety because it is playing catch-up on the business and tech fronts, without a real frontier-lab competitor to U.S. and Chinese firms. Brando Benefei, an Italian MEP, noted that Europe has regulation knowhow but is playing catch-up with the U.S. and China in the race to build out the technology. “Von der Leyen rightfully says that the AI Act positions Europe to lead on AI safety,” he said of the dilemma, while “Europe must [also] now build capacity.” In her 73-minute address von der Leyen devoted a notable portion to AI risk scenarios, citing an incident this summer in which OpenAI-powered agents hacked another AI company, and issuing warnings regarding “self-recursive improvement,” which is when AI models create a smarter version of themselves, leading to an unstoppable loop. The Commission president held the line that the EU executive has been repeating for a week in the face of such threats: We have a law for that. Under the bloc’s four-year-old Artificial Intelligence Act, she said, companies like OpenAI and Anthropic must address the risk of losing control of a model. Von der Leyen largely sidestepped giving her own assessment of whether the development of frontier AI models should be paused, citing calls from tech CEOs to do exactly that. “I will invite the main frontier labs for a discussion on how we can support ongoing industry efforts to pace the frontier,” she said. Advertisement Advertisement But that part of the speech didn’t include an appeal to AI frontrunners U.S. and China, and their leaders Trump and Xi, to act on it — only an offer to middle powers like the U.K. and Canada “and others” to team up on testing the models. Von der Leyen received good marks from MEPs and AI safety experts for her comments on what is within Brussels’ remit, which highlighted the limits on the actions the EU can take. “Finally, the Commission is addressing the frontier risks,” said German Greens lawmaker Sergey Lagodinsky in a statement shared with POLITICO. He praised the “middle powers alliance and dialogue with AI labs” as “the right step.” But he also urged the Commission to “limit the risks” by implementing the AI Act “ambitiously.” Daniel Privitera, executive director of the Berlin-based KIRA Centre AI think tank, commended von der Leyen for acknowledging the risks, but said more is needed than just a meeting. “Inviting CEOs to talk about how Europe can help with efforts to pace the frontier is a first step, but Europe can and should do more to help with a safe transition to transformative AI,” he said. He added that her pitch to team up with the U.K. and Canada to test models is “promising,” as it gives the middle powers “strategic leverage vis-a-vis the two AI superpowers in the world.” But mentioning the testing of models is one thing; promptly creating a mechanism for doing so is quite another. “We urgently need these things,” Privitera said, “as catastrophic risks from frontier AI become more salient.” Advertisement Advertisement

Updated September 7, 2026 at 7:19 PM EDT BERLIN — Germany's populist, far-right Alternative for Germany party has declared victory in the state of Saxony-Anhalt after more than doubling its share of the vote in the first of several regional elections this fall. Falling just shy of an absolute majority, it's not yet clear whether the AfD will be able to govern the state of Saxony-Anhalt. But the outcome is already causing a political earthquake. According to preliminary final results, the AfD won 43.8% of the vote — its strongest performance in any German state election, which puts the far-right party within reach of power for the first time since the time of Nazi Germany. The center-right Christian Democratic Union more than halved its share of the vote, falling to a historic low of 17.2%. The centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) received 9.3%, the Greens 8.9%, and the Left party 8.6%. All of these parties refuse to form a coalition with the AfD. But the AfD can come to power with the help of BSW, a small, anti-immigration, left-wing populist party. BSW got 5.3% of the vote on Sunday, potentially giving it enough seats to form a parliamentary majority with the AfD — something the party has not ruled out. AfD's candidate for state governor, Ulrich Siegmund, said the result "sends a very clear signal to Berlin: this is the end of the line; people don't want to go on like this." "They want their good, old, secure Germany back," Siegmund told German public broadcaster, ARD. Christian Democrat candidate Sven Schulze took to the stage on Sunday evening to congratulate the AfD on its win. While polls had shown the AfD with a comfortable lead for weeks, the CDU fared worse than predicted. Whether Schulze will attempt to cobble together a "firewall" coalition — a platform by Germany's main political parties to keep the AfD out of government — is unclear. Such a strategy would require the Christian Democrats and others to work with the far-left party, Die Linke — something the conservatives refuse to do. Addressing supporters, Schulze sounded resigned. "Some say this is a dark day for Saxony-Anhalt. I say this is democracy," he said. Alice Weidel, co-chair of AfD at the federal level, told public broadcaster ZDF that the CDU will never win another election. She said the AfD is seeing "explosive growth" across the country. In Saxony-Anhalt, that growth is down to 35-year-old Siegmund, a former marketing executive and a salesman who, observers say, showed a knack for packaging his party's policies in positive slogans and pop-star-like appearances at campaign events and on TikTok. His personable and amiable style is uncharacteristically upbeat for the AfD and he distinguishes himself from others in the party for being more happy-go-lucky than angry. Germany's domestic intelligence classifies the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt as extremist. Its regional platform is the party's most radical and is seen by the AfD as a blueprint for the rest of Germany. If Siegmund ends up as state governor, he will be privy to foreign and domestic intelligence, which is a major concern for the other parties considering the AfD's push to revive relations with Russia. Several state interior ministers from Germany's other 15 states say they are already preparing to meet separately. At the top of their platform agenda is what the AfD calls its "remigration" policy, which promises mass deportations. Speaking to public broadcaster ARD on Sunday night, Siegmund spelled out the policy in more detail. "Remigration is far more than just deportation," he said, adding that "remigration applies to anyone who does not contribute to society." He included Ukrainian refugees without jobs. The AfD also wants to segregate refugees and disabled children in schools and revamp the curriculum to focus on what it refers to as a "more positive" teaching of Germany's history. After the results, Siegmund declared: "We have made history in this country." "This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," he told supporters, "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal." On Sunday evening, President Trump posted a screenshot of the projected election results on Truth Social . Trump's post was shared by Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who described the result as a "historic win." The AfD has called for an end to support for Ukraine and seeking to revoke the refugee protections currently granted to Ukrainians. Also among those hailing AfD's success was Tesla CEO Elon Musk. In response, Siegmund thanked Musk for his "support" and "clear and highly important perspective on the political developments of our time." But neighboring Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk took a very different view, posting on X that "in Poland, only idiots or traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD in Germany." France's Europe minister, Benjamin Haddad, described the election results as a " grave moment in Europe ."
